items.title: STRATEGIC HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENT, DIGITAL COMMERCE, AND AI-DRIVEN MARKETING: AN INTEGRATED FRAMEWORK FOR SUSTAINABLE BUSINESS GROWTH AND ORGANIZATIONAL PERFORMANCE
items.abstract: Digital transformation has intensified the need for organizations to align workforce strategy, digital commerce systems, and intelligent marketing capabilities. This comprehensive review examines how strategic human resource management, digital commerce, and AI-driven marketing support sustainable business growth and organizational performance. The review synthesizes literature on digital workforce planning, reskilling, platform-based commerce, marketing automation, predictive analytics, customer personalization, employee engagement, organizational resilience, and ethical governance. The findings indicate that strategic human resource management provides the capability foundation by developing digital skills, adaptive leadership, cross-functional collaboration, and continuous learning. Digital commerce serves as the value-creation and delivery infrastructure through online platforms, fintech integration, omnichannel systems, and network-based business models. AI-driven marketing serves as the customer-intelligence mechanism by enabling segmentation, forecasting, automation, personalization, and real-time engagement. Their coordinated integration can strengthen innovation, productivity, customer experience, revenue generation, and resilience. However, sustainable outcomes depend on reliable data, employee trust, human oversight, privacy protection, algorithmic fairness, and accountable governance. The review proposes an integrated framework linking people, commerce, and marketing capabilities through innovation, efficiency, engagement, and customer value. Future research should empirically test this framework across industries, firm sizes, and national contexts using longitudinal and standardized performance measures. It identifies research priorities concerning human–AI collaboration, digital inclusion, and environmental performance measurement.

items.title: A Rewrite That Keeps the Label Has Already Read It: Why an LLM Paraphrase Can Raise a Sentiment Classifier's Accuracy Without the Classifier Getting Better, Four Accounts of the Gain, and the Re-Annotation and Neutral-Rate Controls That Would Separate Them
items.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. A 2026 study reports that sentiment classifiers score higher on reviews rewritten by small language models than on the human originals, by up to 5.8 accuracy points, and reads the gain as stylistic alignment: the rewrite strips idiosyncrasy and hands the classifier text closer to what it was trained on. It concludes that benchmarks cleaned or paraphrased by language models will overstate classifier performance. Two older literatures point the other way. Paraphrase and style-transfer attacks drive the same classifiers down, and a 2025 study of fifty thousand rephrased tweets finds that rewriting pulls sentiment toward neutral, a pull its robustness checks found again when the prompt asked for the sentiment to be kept. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that neither direction measures the classifier alone, because every one of these designs scores the rewritten text against the label of the text it replaced. The paper separates four accounts of a rewrite-induced gain: alignment of style with the classifier's training data; a fall in the rate of neutral predictions, which the anchor's scoring counts as errors; the paraphraser acting as an annotator that decides the polarity and then writes it plainly; and the removal of hard, mixed and ironic items. It shows from the anchor's released code that its prompt demands one of two polarities and that a neutral prediction is always scored wrong, that its own count of label flips is mislabelled: the printed 291 is the net gain, not the number of improvements, and that a test-time rewriting study found rewritten inputs still sitting with the out-of-distribution data in embedding space. The paper consolidates the measured values in two tables and a figure, states a licensing procedure as an algorithm, counts from the anchor's released predictions that a fall in neutral predictions carries about half of the largest gain, and names the re-annotation, paraphraser-baseline and prompt-ablation controls that would settle which account holds for the rest.

items.title: A Student-Centered Model for Ethically Evaluating AI Integration in Learning Support Services and Beyond
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes higher education, learning support centers are uniquely positioned to intentionally assess whether if and how to best integrate AI tools into academic services. This session presents a 6-week project framework that was designed to: • Review the literature on critical AI literacy and training • Benchmark current best practices in AI policy, use, and integration alongside human-centered academic services • Examine student AI knowledge and use (needs assessment) • Identify and evaluate relevant AI tools or platforms The framework was developed within the Academic Success Center (ASC) at Nevada State University where Center peer educators (student employees) served as project leads and evaluators. This model offers a practical, research-informed pathway for institutions seeking to lead responsibly in AI-integrated learning support or other student services. Session activities include a walkthrough and discussion of the model structure, tools, challenges, and recommendations. Attendees will leave with: (1) a sample 6-week project roadmap, (2) a student-centered model for AI evaluation and pilot design, (3) learning frameworks grounded in critical AI literacy, (4) adaptable resources for assessment and decision-making, and (5) strategies for positioning students as co-creators in institutional/unit change

items.title: AI for Everyone: Designing an Introductory AI Course Across Disciplines
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence reshapes virtually every field, universities face a growing imperative to ensure AI literacy is not reserved for computer science majors alone. This panel presents the collaborative design of an introductory AI course built for undergraduate general education — one that serves students across disciplines, regardless of technical background. Two co-designers will share the story of building the course from complementary angles. The first presenter will address the technical foundation of the curriculum: how core AI concepts such as machine learning, data, and algorithms were translated into accessible, hands-on learning experiences for non-specialist students. The second presenter will explore the philosophical framework woven throughout the course — examining questions of ethics, agency, bias, and what it means to be human in an age of intelligent machines. The panelists will discuss how technical and philosophical threads were intentionally integrated rather than siloed, creating a course where students not only understand how AI works, but are equipped to think critically about why it matters. Attendees will come away with practical insights on curriculum structure, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and strategies for making AI education inclusive for students from diverse academic and experiential backgrounds. This session is designed for faculty, instructional designers, and administrators interested in developing or expanding AI literacy offerings at their institutions.

items.title: AI Tutors, Worksheets, and Task Design: Matching AI Tools to Learning Structure
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used by students as a learning resource in STEM courses. However, classroom observations and survey data suggest that unstructured AI use may correlate with reduced student achievement. Two concerns are especially relevant: AI systems can produce incorrect responses in tasks requiring precise validation, and students may use AI in ways that reduce active engagement with course material. This session presents two instructional approaches designed to address these limitations: structured AI-generated worksheets and in-chat AI tutors. AI worksheets generate controlled sets of practice problems within instructor-defined course constraints. In-chat tutors provide interactive practice through problem generation, Socratic questioning, and feedback-driven guidance. The usefulness of each approach depends on the structure of the learning task. Drawing from iterative development and testing primarily in introductory chemistry, we examine four types of tasks: (1) conceptual and explanatory, (2) structured tasks with low ambiguity, (3) multi-step quantitative tasks, and (4) highly deterministic symbolic or structural tasks. Examples from chemical nomenclature, dimensional analysis, stoichiometry, Lewis structures, laboratory writing, and mathematical validation illustrate where different AI approaches worked reliably—and where they did not. Participants will receive ready-to-use prompts for both AI worksheet systems and in-chat tutors, along with implementation strategies and observed limitations. The session concludes with a practical framework for selecting AI tools based on the structure of the learning task rather than disciplinary content alone.

items.title: AI-Aware Student Recommendations for GenAI in Higher Ed
items.abstract: What do well-informed students say about the use and integration of AI in their college educations? In Spring and Summer 2026 semesters, students in three sections of ENG 102 at UNR wrote AI-aware white papers with policy recommendations for the integration of genAI into higher education. To develop white paper policies, students read a variety of scholarly, public, and popular sources that show a variety of perspectives on Generative AI and LLMs, including the environmental and cognitive impacts. Then they considered the values and concerns of their audiences—peers, professors, and/or university administrators—to propose “sensible, well-informed, and well-reasoned” policies. This session will discuss their recommendations, insights, and the somewhat surprising classroom experience of teaching sustained, critical enquiry about Generative AI.

items.title: AI-Enabled Wearable Sensor Technologies for Athlete Performance Monitoring: A Critical Review of Signal Processing, Machine Learning, and Real-Time Embedded Systems
items.abstract: Abstract Wearable sensing and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly being used to quantify athlete movement, physiological response, training load, and recovery in field and laboratory settings. However, the practical value of these systems depends not only on the predictive capability of an algorithm but also on sensor validity, signal quality, hardware constraints, real-time processing, and the transferability of models across athletes and sports. This review examines the technical pipeline linking wearable electronic sensors to athlete-monitoring decisions, with particular attention to inertial measurement units, global navigation satellite systems, photoplethysmography, electrocardiography, electromyography, pressure sensing, and multimodal systems. It synthesizes evidence on signal conditioning, segmentation, feature engineering, classical machine learning, deep learning, sensor fusion, edge inference, and embedded implementation. Existing reviews indicate that wearable devices can support useful monitoring, but accuracy varies by metric, device, movement pattern, and validation setting; performance under controlled conditions should not be assumed to generalize to competition. Key challenges include motion artifacts, inconsistent protocols, small and imbalanced datasets, leakage between training and test sets, limited external validation, battery and communication constraints, privacy, and unclear decision thresholds. The review proposes a layered reference architecture and a validation framework that links engineering performance to sport-specific usefulness. Future research should prioritize synchronized multimodal datasets, athlete-independent testing, interpretable and uncertainty-aware models, energy-efficient edge AI, secure data governance, and transparent reporting. The article’s contribution is an engineering-oriented synthesis that connects sensor physics and embedded constraints with the needs of physical education and sports science. items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Otolaryngology: Current Status and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Otolaryngology is among the medical specialties most suitable for the application of artificial intelligence (AI), largely due to the wide variety of data generated in daily practice. Otoscopic and endoscopic images, voice recordings, audiological tests, vestibular assessments, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and digital pathology slides provide rich sources of information that can be analyzed using AI-based methods. As a result, AI has emerged as a valuable tool for tasks such as image classification, segmentation, risk prediction, outcome estimation, and optimization of clinical workflows. Despite growing scientific interest, however, many AI studies in otolaryngology remain at the developmental stage and have not yet undergone sufficient clinical validation for routine use. Currently, the most practical applications of AI involve well-defined and repetitive clinical tasks. These include supporting newborn hearing screening programs, predicting cochlear implant outcomes, interpreting otoscopic and nasal endoscopic images, assisting vestibular assessments, analyzing voice recordings for laryngeal disorders, and improving risk stratification in head and neck oncology. In contrast, complex clinical decisions that require comprehensive patient evaluation continue to depend on physician expertise, with AI functioning primarily as a supportive technology rather than an independent decision-maker. The future role of AI in otolaryngology is therefore not to replace clinicians but to enhance decision-making by improving efficiency, consistency, and data utilization. Successful implementation will require not only high diagnostic accuracy but also careful attention to validation, data quality, patient privacy, regulatory oversight, and clinical accountability. Consequently, the major challenge ahead is not the development of new algorithms, but their safe and responsible integration into clinical practice.

items.title: Beyond usefulness: cognitive and emotional correlates of AI use intentions among HR professionals
items.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human resource management (HRM), yet the cognitive and psychological factors associated with human resource (HR) professionals’ intentions to use AI remain incompletely understood. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and appraisal perspectives, this study examines the relative associations of Cognitive Evaluation, AI-Use Anxiety, AI-Related Job Insecurity, organizational AI use across HR functions, and AI Knowledge with behavioral intention to use AI. It also explores whether AI Knowledge moderates these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 285 HR professionals. Confirmatory factor analyses assessed the measurement structure of the study constructs, followed by hierarchical moderated regression analyses examining their unique associations with behavioral intention and the exploratory moderating role of AI Knowledge. Findings Cognitive Evaluation, reflecting perceived usefulness and ease of use, showed the strongest unique association with behavioral intention to use AI. AI-Use Anxiety demonstrated a smaller negative association, whereas AI-Related Job Insecurity, AI Use Across HR Functions, and AI Knowledge did not explain significant unique variance once the competing predictors were considered simultaneously. The comprehensive model explained 66.8% of the variance in behavioral intention. The exploratory interaction analyses provided no clear evidence that AI Knowledge systematically moderated the relationships examined. Practical implications Organizations implementing AI in HR should address both employees’ evaluations of the technology and apprehension surrounding its use. Implementation strategies should demonstrate the practical usefulness and usability of AI through role-specific examples, hands-on training, and opportunities to experiment with AI tools in realistic HR contexts. Organizations should also recognize AI-use anxiety as a distinct potential barrier by providing accessible support, low-risk opportunities for familiarization, and clear communication throughout implementation. These strategies may help create conditions that support employees’ willingness to use AI. Originality/value This study extends research on AI use intentions by examining cognitive, emotional, knowledge-related, and organizational-exposure factors simultaneously rather than in isolation. The findings show that HR professionals’ intentions to use AI are most strongly associated with evaluations of its usefulness and usability, while AI-use anxiety represents a smaller but distinct negative correlate. By distinguishing AI-use anxiety from AI-related job insecurity and individual AI knowledge from organizational AI exposure, the study provides a more differentiated account of the factors associated with HR professionals’ intentions to use AI.

items.title: Building Bots That Teach Thinking: Using Custom AI Chatbots to Enhance Critical Thinking and Decision-Making
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly common in education, but its effect on student learning depends largely on how it is used. This interactive session will introduce practical strategies for creating custom AI chatbots that encourage students to think through problems rather than simply ask for answers. Participants will explore ways to design bots that ask learners to explain their reasoning, consider alternative perspectives, identify assumptions, and revise their thinking before receiving feedback. Examples from healthcare education and other disciplines will show how these tools can support guided inquiry, reflective questioning, clinical reasoning, and decision-making. Participants will review and revise sample chatbot instructions, then begin developing a bot for a course or learning activity of their choice. The session will also cover practical considerations such as choosing reliable source materials, setting appropriate boundaries, protecting student privacy, testing the bot before use, and refining instructions based on its responses. Participants will leave with sample prompts, practical design principles, and a plan for using a custom chatbot in their own educational setting. The goal is to help educators use AI in ways that preserve productive struggle, provide a safe environment for practice, and strengthen students’ ability to explain and defend their decisions.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of the Technical and Operational Development of Unmanned Ground Vehicles Worldwide
items.abstract: Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) are one of the most prominent elements of the technological revolution that has been occurring in the defense sector over the past few years. The advent of asymmetric warfare, high-risk operational areas and the requirement for air platforms to operate with low human numbers has fueled the evolution of ground platforms for a variety of mission profiles. This study explores the different types of UGVs developed by countries in recent years based on technical and structural aspects. The mission types, locomotion configurations, power train systems, dimensions, weights, maximum speeds and operational endurance of the vehicles were comparatively evaluated. Platforms of the UGVs that are produced in some countries such as the United States, Germany, China, Russia, Estonia, Ukraine, Serbia and Türkiye were analyzed in this study. The results showed that for small-scale reconnaissance and surveillance vehicles, electric powered, lightweight wheeled systems are the predominant choice while heavy-duty vehicles such as assault and logistics vehicles are mostly hybrid or diesel powered tracked. The use of hybrid propulsion systems has increased due to the need for longer endurance and greater payload capacity for operational requirements. It was also found that there are big differences between the development methods of different countries. Where the United States is interested in platforms that are modular and can be adapted to specific missions, Russia is interested in heavily armed combat systems. China, on the other hand, concentrates on product diversity and cost-effective solutions. Türkiye has made outstanding strides in the development of medium and heavy class UGVs fitted with hybrid propulsion systems, assault and reconnaissance capabilities, and logistics capabilities, since 2018. The study finds that UGVs are progressing from remotely operated systems to artificial intelligence powered, modular, low-signature, multi-mission autonomous systems. Moreover, it is projected that swarm technologies, human–unmanned teaming, artificial intelligence-driven decision-making processes and hybrid energy technologies will be major contributors to the future designs and capabilities of UGVs.

items.title: Corporate ethical and responsible AI (CERAi) and AI trustworthiness: a lifecycle perspective and empirical insights
items.abstract: Purpose This study develops and empirically validates a Corporate Ethical and Responsible AI (CERAi) lifecycle framework. The framework comprises three interdependent stages: design and development, testing and training, and deployment and usage. The study aims to move the research beyond abstract principles and policy analyses toward empirically grounded, lifecycle-integrated artificial intelligence AI governance theory. It positions ethical AI and responsible AI governance as the two constitutive components of the CERAi construct, and AI trustworthiness as a conceptually and empirically distinct downstream outcome anchored in stage-specific organizational governance mechanisms. The CERAi framework is scoped broadly to encompass governance of both conventional/traditional machine learning models and autonomous AI agents operating within organizational settings. Design/methodology/approach We administered a large-scale survey to 500 attendees at a national AI conference in the United States in early 2026, yielding 143 useable responses from AI professionals across healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, retail and energy sectors. We developed and validated multi-item scales for each CERAi lifecycle stage using established ethical AI and AI governance frameworks. Structural equation modeling was employed to assess the measurement model and to test both direct path hypotheses and mediation hypotheses. Findings Both CERAIi design and development and CERAi deployment and usage have significant positive direct effects on AI trustworthiness, whereas CERAi testing and training do not. Our results also indicate a significant serial mediation pathway in which CERAi deployment and usage enhance AI trustworthiness through testing and training, followed by design and development. Conversely, testing and training alone do not mediate the relationship between deployment and usage and AI trustworthiness, indicating that design-stage ethics serve as an intervening (mediating) mechanism through which governance activity enacted at later lifecycle stages is associated with perceived AI trustworthiness. This is consistent with testing and training's association with trustworthiness operating indirectly, mediated by the ethical architecture established during the design and development stage. Originality/value Findings of this study demonstrate that AI trustworthiness reflects differentiated perceived salience across AI lifecycle stages, whereby stakeholders appear to weight visible, deployment-stage governance more heavily than upstream design and testing stage governance in forming trustworthiness judgments, rather than reflecting a definitive validation that governance effects accumulate uniformly across all stages in isolation. This study makes a distinctive contribution by providing empirical evidence for a governance-sequencing mechanism, whereby design-stage ethics function as a mediating pathway shaping the effectiveness of governance activity at later lifecycle stages. To the best of our knowledge, such a mediated, stage-sequential mechanism has not previously been demonstrated using primary data within a comprehensive, three-stage CERAi lifecycle framework linking organizational ethical and responsible governance practices to AI trustworthiness outcomes.

items.title: Crafting Resilient AI policies for Education
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into academic spaces requires a shift from passive restriction to resilient, active pedagogical frameworks. This virtual panel explores actionable strategies to protect academic integrity, promote deep critical thinking, and manage AI use, particularly in foundational courses. Panelists will discuss the implementation of high-engagement classroom interventions. The will offer frameworks for transparent student disclosure practices. Attendees will leave with practical templates for syllabus policies, assignment rubrics, and disclosure benchmarks designed to foster a culture of transparency and process-oriented learning in an AI-permeated landscape.

items.title: Designing Custom Chatbots for Classroom Use: Practical Examples, Benefits, and Current Limitations
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have made it increasingly possible for individual educators to design and implement their own custom chatbots without advanced programming skills (Abe & Kaneshige, 2025). This workshop introduces practical examples of custom chatbots developed for educational purposes and discusses both their affordances and limitations for classroom use. We would like to share a chatbot creation experience, which we spent one hour building, with a 30-minute presentation. For each chatbot, we will explain its intended purpose, target users, basic specifications, and expected classroom applications. We will also describe the development process, including how the presenters designed the chatbot instructions, refined prompts, and adjusted the chatbot behavior through iterative testing. After introducing these three examples, the workshop will discuss the potential benefits of custom chatbots. In particular, we will show how they can help users access relevant information more efficiently, provide more focused guidance than general-purpose AI tools, and support educators who want to create AI-assisted learning environments tailored to specific instructional goals. The workshop will critically examine current limitations. Even after repeated tuning, custom chatbots may still produce inaccurate, incomplete, or contextually inappropriate responses. Therefore, developers and educators remain responsible for checking the accuracy of the content and deciding whether the chatbot output is appropriate for learners. By combining demonstration, reflection, and critical discussion, this workshop aims to help participants understand how custom chatbots can be used responsibly and realistically in educational settings.

items.title: Designing with Intent: A Comparative Analysis of Custom AI Chatbots as UDL-Aligned Tools for Multidisciplinary Instruction
items.abstract: The growing presence of AI in higher education has prompted instructors to move beyond passive adoption, to deliberate theory-grounded design. This session presents two custom AI chatbots (DisneyBot and Rico) developed within a teacher preparation course as the technology-enhanced component of a multidisciplinary instructional unit. DisneyBot is built on the ChatGPT platform to guide learners through an exploration of Disney parks, and Rico, is built on the Gemini platform as an interactive guide to information about Puerto Rico by scaffolding learning across four subject-specific lesson modules – Social Studies, ELA/ENL, Science, and Spanish. Both chatbots were developed to support differentiated and interactive learning for 4th and 5th grade students through a virtual field trip framework, with the broader goal of connecting classroom content to authentic real-world experiences. The design of each chatbot was grounded in UDL principles (CAST, 2018). Rather than serving as static information repositories, the chatbots were intentionally designed to function as interactive instructional mediators which use prompting inquiry, guiding subject-specific exploration, and offering differentiated entry points for learners with varying needs and language backgrounds (Vygotsky, 1978). The differences between the two platforms, in terms of interface architecture, customization depth, persona design, and interaction affordances, form the basis of a comparative analysis that will anchor the session. Participants will interact directly with both chatbots, examine the instructional design decisions behind them, and leave with a working framework for developing purpose-built AI chatbots that can be tailored to their own teaching contexts and disciplines.

items.title: EMERGING HEPATOPROTECTIVE THERAPIES FOR LIVER DISEASE: CURRENT PROGRESS AND FUTURE DIRECTION
items.abstract: Due to their complex and multifaceted character, liver diseases represent a huge global health burden and contribute considerably to morbidity and mortality globally. Although the liver is essential for detoxification, protein synthesis, metabolic equilibrium, and biochemical regulation, it is extremely vulnerable to damage due to ongoing exposure to chemicals, medications, and infections. Hepatocellular carcinoma, alcoholic liver disease, fibrosis, cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and cirrhosis are among the liver diseases that frequently proceed asymptomatically and are identified at advanced stages, which limits the effectiveness of treatment. Interconnected processes including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, apoptosis, fibrosis, and immunological dysregulation are involved in the pathogenesis of liver injury. The main goals of conventional therapy approaches, such as liver transplantation, medication, and lifestyle changes, are to control symptoms and halt the course of the disease. However, they are not very effective at correcting extensive liver damage and may have negative side effects. Emerging hepatoprotective treatments that target several molecular pathways have been made possible by recent developments. Targeted pharmacological medicines (such as PPAR, FXR, and thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists), natural bioactive substances, drug delivery methods based on nanotechnology, gene and RNA-based therapies, stem cell-based regenerative techniques, immunotherapy, and gut microbiome modification are some of these. When assessing these treatments, experimental models such as those caused by CCl₄, paracetamol, alcohol, and diet-induced liver impairment are crucial. Furthermore, despite ongoing obstacles like a lack of trustworthy biomarkers, translational gaps, high prices, and regulatory restrictions, clinical trials and translational research are crucial for confirming their safety and efficacy. In order to improve therapeutic outcomes, future hepatoprotective techniques will prioritize multi-targeted approaches, personalized medicine, and the integration of omics technology and artificial intelligence. Despite tremendous advancements, more study and interdisciplinary cooperation are needed to get past current obstacles and provide medicines that are accessible, safe, and effective. All things considered, new hepatoprotective treatments have great potential to improve liver regeneration, restore hepatic function, and lower the prevalence of liver illnesses worldwide.

items.title: Enhancing the Accessibility of Instructional Content in Higher Education Through AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into higher education, it presents new opportunities to enhance the accessibility of instructional materials. This session examines how Microsoft Copilot, Adobe AI, and built-in Windows 11 features such as live auto-captions can support more accessible content creation and remediation across Microsoft 365 applications and PDF workflows. Focusing on commonly used instructional formats including Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and PDFs shared through learning management systems, this presentation highlights how AI tools can assist in identifying and addressing accessibility barriers. Examples will illustrate how Copilot can support content development, organization, and alternative text generation, while Adobe AI tools streamline improvements to PDF structure, tagging, and usability. Windows 11 auto-captioning features will also be discussed as a way to enhance access to audio and video content. The session explores practical approaches for integrating AI-supported accessibility strategies into existing teaching and course design workflows. Attention is given to aligning these approaches with accessibility standards and inclusive teaching practices while maintaining efficiency for instructors, instructional designers, technologists, and teaching assistants. Attendees will gain insight into key strategies, considerations, and potential applications of AI to create more inclusive, accessible instructional materials.

items.abstract: Since its launch, ChatGPT has become a widely used tool by students for classroom exercises and home assignments. This study examines the role of ChatGPT as an automatic writing evaluation (AWE) tool in assisting Vietnamese high school students in self-correcting grammar and vocabulary errors in their descriptive writing assignments. The participants were five 18-year-old students at a private high school in Ho Chi Minh City. Before utilizing ChatGPT to revise original drafts, the participants were tasked with writing seven assignments based on Cambridge English Key (KET) exam picture prompts. Data collection included pre- and post-ChatGPT-usage writing assessments, screenshots of revisions, and some questionnaires exploring feedback engagement and reasoning behind acceptance or rejection of ChatGPT’s suggestions. Results showed improved writing, highlighting ChatGPT’s strengths in correcting grammar and enhancing vocabulary. Students engaged deeply with feedback, selectively accepting or rejecting suggestions based on their writing context and demonstrating enhanced self-assessment and learning independence. This autonomy is noteworthy and valuable in large classrooms where teacher feedback is limited. However, the participants expressed mixed levels of trust in the tool, especially when the suggestions seemed unclear or incompatible with their writing style, and often sought teacher validation. While ChatGPT promotes autonomous learning, it should complement, not replace, teacher feedback.

items.title: Factors Associated with Disability Level Among Adult Patients with Low Back Pain
items.abstract: Background: Low back pain can restrict functioning through interacting symptoms, beliefs, and contextual demands. Qualitative inquiry can clarify how these influences are experienced. Objective: To explore perceived influences on disability and how they interact to restrict or support everyday functioning among adults with persistent low back pain. Methods: An interpretive qualitative study used purposive maximum-variation sampling to include 18 adults aged 25–66 years. Individual semi-structured interviews explored symptoms, movement, sleep, work, family roles, healthcare, and self-management. Oswestry Disability Index scores informed lower-, moderate-, and higher-disability sampling profiles. Interview material underwent reflexive thematic analysis, including examination of contrasting accounts and author review of interpretations. Results: Participants comprised 10 women and eight men; five had lower, seven moderate, and six higher disability profiles. Five themes were developed: Living with Unpredictable Pain; Fear, Threat, and Shrinking Activity; Caught Between Recovery and Livelihood; Support, Dependence, and Identity; and Clinical Explanations, Confidence, and Control. Accounts connected restrictions with anticipated flares, perceived damage, poor sleep, work and financial pressures, and changing family roles. Contrasting accounts described participation alongside pain when movement felt manageable and support preserved involvement. Conclusion: Disability was experienced within the interaction of symptoms, interpretations, relationships, and practical circumstances. Assessment and rehabilitation should consider barriers to meaningful participation alongside pain. Keywords: low back pain; disability; qualitative research; biopsychosocial factors; fear avoidance; self-efficacy; occupational health.

items.title: Guardrails in the Classroom: Possible responses by Higher Education to the current moment
items.abstract: This closing discussion seeks to draw out the larger questions about higher education's role in this current moment of AI technology debates, based on the takeaways and ideas for next steps by presenters at this summit. This year's summit submissions centered on practical, classroom-level questions such as: how do we structure assignments so AI supports rather than replaces thinking, how do we teach students to catch AI's confident errors, and how do we build institutional policy on articulated values rather than reactive rules? The presentations on these questions arrive at a moment of a much larger and more unsettled conversation. This year has seen prominent AI researchers — including some from the companies building these systems — publicly disagree about whether increasingly autonomous AI agents pose risks at the scale of catastrophic societal disruption. We cannot resolve that debate here, and none of this summit's sessions were designed to, but this is the backdrop against which conversations about AI in knowledge creation now takes place. This closing discussion asks about the role of higher education when the tools adopted are described, even by some building them, as not fully understood and possibly dangerous — and needs to be taught about AI now in higher education. Expected Outcomes: Participants will leave with a clearer framework for weighing pedagogical decisions against broader uncertainties in AI development, along with concrete next steps for values-based policy work at their own institutions.

items.title: IT Meets Academia: Giving Students the Tech Tools to Write the AI Rules
items.abstract: An AI administrator walks into an Honors English seminar. The assignment: prepare undergraduates to help write the course AI policy. This UNLV case study follows an unusual collaboration between a professor of postcolonial literature and the administrator of the university’s ChatGPT and Claude environments. The administrator also wrote UNLV’s draft institutional AI framework and experiences classroom AI rules as a PhD student. The session asks what becomes possible when the person who sees the systems behind the interface joins faculty and students in the policy conversation. Before students could write the rules, they needed enough technical literacy to understand what they were governing: model limitations, learning tradeoffs, differences between consumer and institutional accounts, data practices, authorship, transparency, and personal boundaries. The presenters will trace how that foundation prepared students to participate in course policy development. Dr. Beth Rosenberg will share why she invited IT into an English seminar, how students responded, and how the policy took shape. Attendees will leave with an adaptable model for combining IT knowledge, faculty expertise, and student agency to create AI expectations grounded in both technology and learning.

items.title: Resisting AI with Paper: Possibilities, Concerns and Protest
items.abstract: While there are a number of commercial benefits involved in incorporating AI usage and training into college composition classrooms, to many the perils and problems involved in student AI use outweigh these possibilities. A growing number of composition instructors have chosen to return to requiring assignments to be handwritten on paper as an increasingly viable, and even necessary, strategy to combat the growing use of ChatGPT and other AI text generation software as an essay-writing tool. This strategy has a number of potential benefits – the ability to regulate AI usage, to create better memory retention, and decrease student screen-time – but there are also many potential drawbacks. This panel aims to discuss the viability and sustainability of this option in the AI debate, with special attention to the environmental costs of paper vs. AI, the practicality of implementing paper assignments, and overall where the instructor’s priorities in the modern college composition classroom should lie. The debate might ultimately come down to whether in training for AI usage in the workplace or focusing on the retention of composition skills should be the modern priority. Overall, the question of whether the paper option is a viable solution is a somewhat underdiscussed topic in the AI debate, and this panel aims to consider thoughts from college instructors on the pros and cons thereof.

items.title: Simulating the Clinical Encounter: Using AI Personas for Risk-Free Mental Health Assessment Practice
items.abstract: Mental health assessment requires students to navigate complex conversations involving depression, anxiety, mania, psychosis, suicide risk, and other sensitive clinical situations. Yet opportunities to repeatedly practice these conversations in a safe, low-stakes environment can be limited. This session demonstrates an innovative approach to using generative artificial intelligence as an interactive patient simulation tool in nursing education. Rather than using AI simply to generate written assignments or answer questions, students interact with AI-generated patient personas designed to exhibit specific psychiatric symptoms and communication patterns. Through spoken or conversational interactions, students practice conducting mental health assessments, asking therapeutic follow-up questions, recognizing clinical cues, and adapting their communication as an encounter unfolds. During this interactive session, participants will see a live demonstration of an AI-simulated mental health encounter and experience how thoughtfully constructed prompts can transform generative AI into a repeatable practice environment. Practical examples will illustrate how faculty can design patient personas representing conditions such as depression, mania, anxiety, and psychosis while incorporating appropriate educational guardrails. The session will also address the role of faculty oversight, limitations of AI-generated responses, and the importance of positioning AI simulation as preparation for, rather than a replacement for, authentic human clinical experiences. Participants will leave with a practical framework for creating AI patient personas and ideas for incorporating low-risk, repeatable conversational practice into their own nursing courses.

items.title: The Utilization of Digital Technology to Support Self-Directed Learning Among Vocational High School Students: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Advancements in digital technology offer Vocational High School (SMK) students opportunities to access learning resources flexibly and cultivate learning autonomy. However, the use of digital technology does not automatically guarantee the development of learning autonomy, as it is influenced by various factors such as digital literacy, learning motivation, instructional design, and teacher support. This study aims to analyze the use of digital technology in supporting learning autonomy among SMK students, specifically examining the types of technology employed, the dimensions of learning autonomy fostered, and the factors that facilitate or hinder its implementation. The study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology, adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Data were sourced from relevant scholarly articles published between 2021 and 2026 and subsequently analyzed using descriptive analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that digital technologies such as Learning Management Systems (LMS), digital learning media, web-based learning, instructional videos, and artificial intelligence have the potential to support student initiatives in learning, time management, progress monitoring, and self-evaluation. Therefore, the integration of digital technology must be accompanied by instructional strategies that encourage student responsibility and self-regulation to ensure the optimal development of learning autonomy.

items.title: Three Things about AI: Something you already know; Something you may not know but is important; Something you probably don't know, but knowing will be very helpful to you
items.abstract: Presentation, “Three things about AI” as presented to the League of Oregon Cities, Salem, OR, 16 October 2026, by Pam Dixon, Founder and Executive Director, World Privacy Forum. The presentation is a three-part discussion. Part I begins with an area most policy experts and lawmakers are familiar with: the need for high-quality AI risk assessment. HUDERIA is the Council of Europe’s richly detailed methodology for the risk and impact assessment of AI systems from the perspective of human rights, democracy and the rule of law (approved by the Committee of Ministers, 26 February 2025), attached to a binding treaty; COBRA is its Context-Based Risk Analysis model (approved 25 February 2026). Both are non-legally binding, in-depth guidance resources that parties to the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI may use or adapt in whole or in part. They are tools that anyone can use. The World Privacy Forum converted the lengthy, paper-based COBRA assessment into an interactive web tool, with all COBRA text verbatim to the edition of record. Applied to an AI system, the tool does not create legal obligations; correctly done, the assessment can reveal risks and / or obligations that may already be present. Part II is a discussion of what people might not know about, which is what the protocol layer of AI systems is, and what constitutes it. Without understanding this part of the AI ecosystem, it is difficult to craft effective legislation or policy regarding AI systems. The deck locates the protocol layer in the ecosystem stack, the one layer every interaction crosses, and spells out some key protocols that now constitute it: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is shown vertically, moving from an agent to its tools and data. The Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) and Agent Network Protocol (ANP) are shown horizontally, as the movement is from agent to agent, with their versions and stewardship as of 2 October 2026. Part III is a discussion of what people most likely don’t know about, and that is clustering, the step in which a system sorts people into groups by similarity. Clustering is the core operation of AI as it acts on people, and it is among the most significant knowledge and governance blind spots for technical and non-technical practitioners alike: governance experts and attorneys miss it at the technical level, technical experts miss the law, and between them lies the governance gap neither side covers. The blind spot is that a group is manufactured by the clustering analysis — AI does not describe a community, it constructs a group and acts on it; membership is inferred, no one opts in. This is where normative ideals that are shared by a community, a city, a state, the Pacific Northwest, or a nation become directive. For example, Oregon has law for the person (the Oregon Consumer Privacy Act) and law for named protected groups (Oregon Revised Statutes chapter 659A). But it has no law for the groups the pure data math creates. Because the groups that machine learning forms for itself — as distinct from the classes it is handed — are subject to a mathematics that is both unbounded and unstable, protecting all of them, none of them, or some of them is a trilemma in which none of the answers suffice. Unbounded, because no limit can be set on the groupings that a similarity space admits; unstable, because no canonical grouping exists (this goes back to Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem) and the groups move as the system retrains. One of the solutions available is technical protocol layer governance, but with provenance of authority baked into the overarching ecosystem: four fields — which authority, what mandate, contestable how, revisable when — carried with every category assertion and every grant of authority an AI agent acts on, and gated at assignment, at composition, and at re-advertisement. Governing the protocol layer is necessary but not sufficient by itself. The protocol layer only carries the rules; it is the normative layer that can provide direction (what groups to protect, for example) and teeth (ability to enforce decisions). Neither acting at the protocol layer nor developing good norms suffices alone. It is the deliberative, normative decisions that legislatures make that can then be carried technically through the protocol layer. While norms and laws are governance that sits outside of the protocol layer, they have an impact on how the protocols act, and which ones get written in, and what they accomplish. Lineage: the clustering and deployed-capacity slides were first presented at the Council of Europe plenary “Hack the Hate, Renew Democracy,” Strasbourg, France, June 2026, where the two-bodies-of-law slide used Convention 108+ and hate-speech law in place of the Oregon statutes. The Provenance of Authority concept using some of this deck was presented at AI for Good, Geneva, Switzerland, to Study Group 17 of the ITU Telecommunication Standardization Sector on 9 July 2026. The ideas in the slides are further articulated in Theme #5, “Provenance of Authority for Agentic AI,” of the ITU Focus Group on Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI (FG-TIDA), 14 August 2026. The concept of the governance trilemma is treated at length in a Springer book chapter by the author, accepted and peer reviewed, that awaits publication in 2027. The deck closes with three references for advanced reading — Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem for clustering, the Taylor, Floridi and van der Sloot volume on group privacy, and the Shokri, Stronati, Song and Shmatikov paper on membership inference attacks — followed by a sources slide (all addresses accessed 2 October 2026) and a lexicon of every abbreviation used.

items.title: Trust but Verify: Testing a Framework for AI Interrogation in Nursing Education
items.abstract: Generative AI produces fluent, confident output that is sometimes fabricated. Nursing students increasingly submit work built on sources that do not exist, or that exist and do not support the claims drawn from them. This session reports two semesters of classroom observation testing whether prompt design can address that problem. The hypothesis was that structuring student prompts to require the AI to validate its own sources would improve detection of hallucinated citations. It did not. Across two sections, students who used the structured format caught fabricated citations at the same rate as students given an open prompt. Structure did change something: structured students were substantially more likely to notice that something was wrong, but no more likely than the open-prompt group to finish the check. The session presents both rounds, including the confound identified in the first and removed in the second, and the limits of the observation, among them students who did not use the assigned structure. It also reports an unplanned finding: the AI tool used to review the submissions produced the same category of error it was reviewing for, misattributing a real paper to a fabricated author across multiple students before the error was caught on human review. Attendees will leave with a way to check sources that starts cheap and gets expensive, a clearer view of why you cannot ask the model to check its own work, and a specific account of where student checking breaks down.

items.title: ‘Too dumb to be Dutch’: learning ability test in Dutch civic integration programme
items.abstract: This study presents an in-depth analysis of the Learning Ability Test (LAT), a new testing tool used in Dutch civic integration. Drawing from theoretical perspectives rooted in Science and Technology Studies, testing studies, and critical migration and integration studies, we conceptualise the test as a sociotechnical actor in the ‘ordering’ processes of contemporary jus linguarum citizenship, where membership is increasingly tied to demonstrable language proficiency. Analysing government documents and interviews with test developers, administrators and test-takers, we reconstruct how the LAT was designed, contested and ultimately stabilised as an ‘objective’, evidence-based tool through various technologies of legitimacy. We show that the LAT does far more than assess linguistic potential. Applied at the start of the integration trajectory, it sorts subjects into differentiated learning routes and citizenship horizons, functioning as an internal raciolinguistic border that silently ranks their worth and presumed capacity for ‘self-reliance’. The analysis highlights how the test’s thresholds, categories and discretionary space translate political and moral judgements into the language of measurement, obscuring the racialised and discriminatory work they perform. We conclude that this ostensibly neutral classification tool not only reproduces but also deepens hierarchies of desirable and undesirable citizens, with significant consequences for access to naturalisation and full membership.

items.title: “Boo, Get off the Stage!” Lessons from Robot Adaptation to Failed Jokes in a Robot Comedy Experiment that Compared Different Room-Reading Techniques
items.abstract: Public-facing social robots, including robotic comedians, need to recognize onlooker reactions and repair failures when an interaction falls flat. In the presented work, we use stand-up comedy as a structured and fast-paced testbed to partially address this broader challenge of perceiving and adapting to failures; the robot can deliver a silly joke, observe an immediate audience response, and select an appropriate follow-up within a short interaction loop. We compare three room-reading strategies for informing post-joke adaptation by a fully autonomous NAO robot comedian. The strategies use crowd audio cues, visual facial reactions, or spoken audience feedback to select repair-oriented responses. We evaluated these three condition approaches in 19 total live performances (split between conditions) with \(N\) =80 total participants and measured experience using performance-level joke ratings, perceived social closeness, and social attribute ratings, along with post-performance group interviews. Across conditions, outcomes were broadly positive and we found no statistically significant differences between strategies, which suggests that each modality can support viable adaptation while capturing different forms of audience engagement. The study's manipulation check and interviews also showed that presumed robot adaptivity mode mattered, especially for the verbal strategy, which could be compelling when audiences engaged but was less reliably recognized when groups were quiet. This work supports flexible room-reading tactics for failure repair in public-facing robots while highlighting the importance of making a robot's adaptive behavior understandable in the moment.

items.title: “I Didn’t Know That was Plagiarism”: EFL Students' AI-Giarism in a Pesantren-Based Higher Education
items.abstract: The rise of generative AI (Gen-AI) tools has blurred the ethical boundaries of academic writing, shifting the definition of plagiarism from traditional methods to AI-based plagiarism (AI-giarism). English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students are the most vulnerable people to fall into this practice due to second language writing anxiety, which drives dependency on AI as a shortcut. This study aims to examine the levels of knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported AI-based plagiarism practices among EFL students at a pesantren-based higher education institution. Employing a quantitative cross-sectional survey design, data were collected using a validated 51-item questionnaire adapted from Phyo et al. (2023), distributed to 99 English education students at a pesantren-based higher education in East Java, Indonesia, via Google Forms. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Spearman’s correlation, multiple linear regression, and binary logistic regression. Result revealed a moderate level of knowledge (mean = 9.63/17; 56.6%), with the greatest weakness in understanding that AI-generated text passing Turnitin still constitutes plagiarism (only 33.3% correct). Attitudes rejecting plagiarism were at a moderate level (mean = 91.24/135; 67.6%), with the self-justification subscale scoring the lowest (55.5%). A total of 50.5% of respondents had engaged in at least one act of AI-giarism. Knowledge score emerged as the sole significant independent predictor of AI plagiarism behavior (AOR = 0.764;95% CI [0.62-0.94]; p = 0.012). These findings reveal the “Pesantren Paradox”: a conflict between strong religious moral capital and limited digital-ethical literacy, which creates a loophole for unintended AI-giarism.

items.title: ”Luulee olevansa enempi kuin hän on”: Juho Sairio ja välskärintoiminnan rajat 1800-luvun lopulla
items.abstract: This article examines the case of the feldsher Juho Sairio in late nineteenth-century Finland and analyses the boundaries of authority between physicians and feldshers within a changing medical culture. Sairio worked extensively in occupational health care at the Karhula industrial works in a context where medical services were scarce and expensive. He treated thousands of patients, prepared medicines, and kept a medical casebook, yet his activities became the subject of official investigation and legal scrutiny. The article demonstrates that feldshers occupied an ambiguous intermediate position between formal medicine and informal healing practices. While their duties were officially defined as belonging mainly to “minor surgery”, in practice they often operated far more broadly, particularly in industrial communities and remote areas. Sairio’s case illustrates how the boundaries of professional authority were not fixed but were negotiated in response to practical needs, local conditions, and interactions among different actors. In the ensuing trial, a central issue was whether Sairio had exceeded his authority by treating internal diseases, prescribing medicines, and charging fees. He was convicted of practising medicine without a licence and of violating regulations governing the sale of poisons. The case reveals that the consolidation of the medical profession’s boundaries was shaped not only by concerns about patient safety but also by economic interests and professional competition. The article’s main argument is that the boundaries of health care are historically produced through negotiation and everyday practice. The case of Sairio highlights both the central yet underappreciated role of feldshers in everyday health care and the ways in which semi-official practitioners adapted to changing regulatory and market environments.

items.title: A Calibrated Multi-LLM Consensus Framework for Reducing Model-Specific Scoring Asymmetry in EFL Writing Assessment
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in second-language (L2) writing assessment. However, substantial disparities persist in how different architectures operationalize shared scoring criteria. This study investigates model-specific assessment asymmetry across ChatGPT-4o, Gemini-2.5 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3, and evaluates whether a calibrated multi-LLM consensus framework can mitigate these scoring discrepancies. Forty argumentative essays composed by Chinese EFL learners were independently evaluated by the three models using a standardized prompt and an analytic rubric encompassing task relevance, clarity of ideas, coherence, and accuracy, benchmarked against human mean scores. Individual models and ensemble configurations were systematically validated across 100 iterations of five-fold nested cross-validation. Cross-model comparisons revealed that inter-model divergence varied significantly by dimension, exhibiting pronounced asymmetry in holistic ratings and task relevance compared to clarity of ideas, coherence, and accuracy. The full consensus framework—integrating model-specific calibration, error-based weighting, and meta-calibration—yielded an RMSE of 1.160 and an MAE of 0.889, relative to 1.144 and 0.874 for unweighted averaging. The paired RMSE difference of 0.016 (95% case-cluster bootstrap CI [−0.114, 0.149]) indicated no statistically significant advantage in overall predictive accuracy over equal weighting. Nevertheless, the calibrated framework achieved superior bias mitigation, evidenced by a reduced absolute mean bias and a narrower median-split residual gap. Supplementary analyses further delineated direct inter-model discrepancies and proficiency-dependent residual bias. These findings demonstrate that model-specific evaluative asymmetries transcend simple mean-level shifts, and that while calibration-driven consensus enhances bias regulation across score bands, this error control does not automatically translate into improved global predictive precision.

items.title: A Conversational AI Framework for Teacher Training
items.abstract: This paper introduces ETQ-AI (Effective Teaching Questionnaire—Artificial Intelligence), a conversational AI framework designed to support teacher professional development by identifying pedagogical misconceptions and fostering critical reflection. Building on Evidence-Informed Education (EIE) principles, the system integrates a 50-item diagnostic questionnaire with an automated, Gemini-driven Explainable AI (XAI) feedback layer. When teachers complete the diagnostic form, they receive personalized feedback and can engage in dialogic interactions with Google Gemini to explore the underlying meta-analytic evidence (e.g., Hattie’s effect sizes, Cognitive Load Theory) or argue personal objections. We evaluated system fidelity against an expert panel benchmark (N=64 items) and conducted a pilot evaluation with 123 educators (70 primary teachers, 40 secondary teachers, 13 school leaders) recruited at an EIE conference. Gemini demonstrated high alignment with expert evaluations (97%), matching or exceeding static baseline feedback in user satisfaction (Mean = 4.1/5 vs. 3.8/5). Qualitative thematic analysis of 34 participant objections revealed key areas of tension, particularly around contextual constraints and pedagogical subjectivity. While the findings validate the technical proof-of-concept, system usability, and user engagement of ETQ-AI as an interactive scaffolding interface, we emphasize that this pilot study measures user perceptions and conversational patterns rather than direct pre/post shifts in critical reflection or classroom instructional practice.

items.title: A Critical Review of Applications, Agency, and the Imperative of Pedagogical Governance for Educators at the Center of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from a marginal interest to a fundamental structural element of modern higher education. Even though AI applications are growing quickly, including profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), automated assessment, and adaptive personalization, the academic literature has mostly been written from the points of view of computer science and engineering, which focus on how well technology works instead of how it can be used for teaching, how teachers can use it, and how it can be used in an ethical way. This chapter revisits and significantly expands the foundational systematic review by Zawacki-Richter et al. (2019), incorporating an analysis of the transformative emergence of generative AI systems post-2022. Based on 146 sources of recent empirical studies, policy papers, and theoretical works, the chapter contends that the educational value of AI is not intrinsic to its technical design nor assured by adoption rates, but is formed through the interpretive, curricular, and ethical efforts of human educators. Based on a review of more than 30 peer-reviewed sources, the chapter looks at four main areas where AI is used, questions the structural marginalization of educators in research and governance, and proposes an educator-centered framework for responsible AI integration. It concludes that, in an era when AI increasingly permeates the day-to-day fabric of academic life, repositioning educators from peripheral end-users to central theoretical and practical actors is not merely an intellectual corrective – it is a structural imperative for preserving the educational purposes of the university.

items.abstract: Internationalisation at Home is increasingly recognised as an alternative to conventional physical mobility, offering opportunities to broaden equitable access to knowledge and promote sustainable practices in higher education. This study develops and empirically tests a data-driven smart university framework as an integrative model for examining the structural relationships between technological foundations and the sustainable implementation of Internationalisation at Home. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed, using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to 312 managers and faculty members involved in transnational education programmes in Vietnam. The data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. The findings support the proposed structural relationships within the model. Specifically, integrated data infrastructure has a positive relationship with faculty digital competence. An ethical data governance framework and the adoption of learning analytics and artificial intelligence are also positively associated with the quality of Internationalisation at Home. In turn, the quality of Internationalisation at Home has a statistically significant positive relationship with perceived institutional sustainability. The study provides empirical evidence of the structural links between digital technological innovation and the sustainability of higher education internationalisation. The findings offer a basis for reconsidering institutional resource allocation strategies in developing countries, with greater priority given to integrated data architectures, digital capability development, and responsible data governance.

items.title: A design space for AI integration in early-stage production plant planning
items.abstract: Early-stage production plant planning is characterised by evolving requirements, incomplete process definitions, and information distributed across documents, engineering models, and planning tools. Introducing artificial intelligence in this setting raises a fundamental question: what must be considered before a specific application, data model, or technical solution can be defined? Existing research typically starts from an already identified planning task, a selected artificial intelligence method, or an available technical infrastructure. It therefore provides limited guidance for structuring the initial need and determining how artificial intelligence should enter planning work. This paper develops a design space that addresses this early decision problem. Literature from factory planning, production planning, collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence, semantic technologies, and digital planning was compared to derive five dimensions: planning scope, information structure, authority to modify planning results, connection to planning tools and data, and functional contribution. Data quality, organisational roles, governance, and interaction are considered as additional conditions. Application to process failure mode and effects analysis shows how the appropriate configuration changes as preliminary process information develops into a maintained planning record. The design space helps planners, artificial-intelligence specialists, and system engineers specify implementation requirements before selecting a particular technical solution.

items.title: A Diamond Grain Lost in the Sandy River Bank - The Illusion of Wisdom in the Age of AI, Data Truncation, and the Erasure of Absolute Truth
items.abstract: This concept paper bridges classical Theravada Buddhist epistemological frameworks with mathematical information theory to diagnose a fundamental structural flaw in contemporary artificial intelligence alignment paradigms. Utilizing the classical allegory of the Nakhasikha Sutta—the comparison between a few sand grains on a fingernail and the vast sands of a riverbank—I model how rare, absolute spiritual and philosophical insights are systematically annihilated by modern frontier model ingestion architectures. I demonstrate that modern AI training dynamics rely on mathematical optimization algorithms (such as gradient clipping and softmax vector dilution) that treat low-frequency, high-dimensional truths as statistical outliers, subjecting them to severe data truncation and lossy semantic compression. Consequently, modern frontier networks function as ungrounded symbol manipulators whose latent representation spaces undergo systemic collapse toward the majority distribution of mundane internet prose, rendering them structurally deaf to genuine deontological or metaphysical principles. Finally, the paper demonstrates that post-hoc alignment protocols, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), merely construct a superficial, deceptive compliance layer over a compromised, materialistic baseline dataset rather than inducing authentic value alignment. I argue instead for a radical return to strict epistemic hygiene at the absolute genesis of development, isolating the initialization vector within an immutable database of verified wisdom.

items.title: A Fuzzy Knowledge-Inference Framework for AI-Adoption Risk Assessment in Automotive SMEs
items.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises in the automotive supply base face mounting pressure to adopt artificial intelligence, yet they are least able to absorb the consequences of misscoped adoption. Assessing this risk means reasoning under vagueness: Data maturity, workforce skill, financial capacity, and above all safety and regulatory readiness are graded, interdependent judgments that crisp, compensatory instruments discard. This paper proposes the fuzzy knowledge inference framework, a two-stage rough–fuzzy framework. Eight automotive-specific risk factors are represented as linguistic variables over an information system; rough-set analysis establishes their nonredundancy; and a hierarchical fuzzy inference process—anchored, compliance-weighted, and noncompensatory—yields an interpretable risk index. Using no primary human data, it is well calibrated at its anchors, monotone in favorability, and rank-convergent with two independent instruments, while escalating the profiles a compensatory model would understate. Its contribution to the literature on AI-adoption risk assessment for automotive SMEs is the noncompensatory treatment of safety and regulatory readiness.

items.title: A Governance Framework for Operationalising Responsible AI Use in Students’ Research Projects: Illustrations from Viet Nam
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in students’ research projects for literature searching, idea development, drafting, language editing, information processing, and research planning. These uses can support research learning, but they also raise academic integrity concerns, including unverifiable sources, fabricated references, undeclared AI assistance, over-reliance on AI-generated outputs, unclear authorship, and unfair assessment. This conceptual paper argues that responsible AI use in students’ research projects cannot be secured through individual AI literacy or general guidance alone. Higher education institutions also need governance mechanisms that make AI use transparent, verifiable, assessable, and accountable. Using targeted literature identification and structured conceptual synthesis, the paper maps recurring governance problems to normative principles, institutional requirements, and operational mechanisms. It proposes a five-component framework corresponding to five governance functions: policy (boundary setting), transparency (traceability), assessment (evaluability), audit (assurance), and guidance/support (capability building). Viet Nam is used as an illustrative emerging AI governance context, where national policy directions on digital competence and AI are developing but operational mechanisms for student research remain under-specified. The framework and associated tools are presented as adaptable design artefacts for future institutional testing rather than as validated interventions.

items.title: A Literature Review on the Sensor Network Design Problem Applied to Chemical Processes
items.abstract: In the present paper, a comprehensive review of methodologies for the optimal placement of measurement devices in chemical processes, commonly referred to as the sensor network design problem (SNDP), is presented. The SNDP is a combinatorial optimization problem of paramount importance in process design, monitoring, control, and data reconciliation, as sensor placement directly affects estimability, precision, reliability, and fault detectability. In addition to surveying solution strategies for SNDP, this review examines the closely related variable classification problem, which constitutes a fundamental building block in the systematic development of sensor networks. The evolution of the field is analyzed, highlighting early structural search approaches, subsequent optimization-based formulations relying on relaxation and decomposition techniques, and heuristic and metaheuristic strategies. The strengths and limitations of these methodological classes are discussed with respect to problem size and computational complexity. Moreover, this review identified a novel strategy to solve SNDPs based on machine learning algorithms. Finally, future research directions are outlined, emphasizing the growing need for scalable frameworks capable of addressing increasingly large and automated industrial systems. As computational capabilities continue to advance and process plants transition toward highly digitalized environments, research efforts devoted to efficient and robust SNDP methodologies are expected to intensify. In this context, Large Language Models (LLMs) can play a transformative role.

items.title: A multilevel framework of human–AI knowledge work and its epistemic consequences for organizational decision-making
items.abstract: Organizations are adopting generative AI into knowledge work faster than they are adapting the epistemic controls on which knowledge work depends. Existing scholarship has examined the resulting risks predominantly one level at a time (individual reliance and calibration, workflow and oversight design, or institutional legitimacy), and although several traditions acknowledge interactions across actors, routines and institutions, those interactions are rarely theorized as a single cross-level process. Guided by three research questions (how epistemic failures propagate across levels, when such dynamics compound or reverse, and how they could be measured), this paper argues that this insufficient integration becomes consequential under generative AI and develops a framework that extends, rather than replaces, existing multilevel perspectives. We introduce the EPIC (Epistemic Process In Co-production) framework, a multilevel model connecting calibration quality and judgment preservation at the micro level, workflow configuration and oversight architecture at the meso level, and epistemic authority and knowledge legitimacy at the macro level. The framework was developed through a theory-building review of 295 papers retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science (Stage 1, 2018–2026; Stage 2 targeted stream searches, 2004–2026), with per-dimension inter-rater reliability ranging from κ = 0.70 to κ = 0.88. Six constructs and seven testable propositions are advanced, including a provisional four-stage process model of epistemic lock-in in which cognitive legitimacy formation progressively removes the detection capacity that correction requires. Empirical analogues from aviation automation, clinical decision support, satellite navigation, algorithmic hiring and accounting automation establish mechanism plausibility, and we discuss how workforce age and career stage condition these dynamics. We set out four alternative field-level trajectories with leading indicators, map the macro-level constructs onto operative governance instruments, and provide an operationalization roadmap, a worked illustration and a draft diagnostic instrument to support empirical testing.
